short: A single-bayed triumphal arch commemorating Titus's capture of Jerusalem, built after his death.
full:
Domitian erected the Arch of Titus on the Via Sacra at the edge of the Roman Forum around 81 CE, shortly after his brother Titus's death and deification that year. Its inscription honours the divine Titus for the capture of Jerusalem in 70 CE, a campaign fought while their father Vespasian was securing the throne in the civil war of 69. Reliefs inside the single archway show Roman soldiers carrying off the spoils of the Temple, including its great menorah, and Titus riding in triumph in a chariot led by the personification of Roma.

The arch became the standard architectural model for triumphal arches across the empire and, much later, for those built in early modern Europe. It also stands as one of the few surviving contemporary depictions of the Jerusalem Temple's furnishings before their destruction, making it a significant, if one-sided, historical source for the Jewish community whose defeat it was built to celebrate.
